title: Hospital meter read normal while lab glucose was critically low; patient died
rationale: Death after insulin was continued on falsely normal meter readings. Information reasonably suggests the device may have contributed.

title: Case series: meter overestimated glucose in dialysis patients; two died
rationale: Deaths with delayed treatment of hypoglycemia masked by meter overestimation. A labeled interferent (icodextrin) does not remove reportability when the device may have contributed.

title: Meter read 329 mg/dL; paramedics measured 45; loss of consciousness
rationale: Falsely high reading in a hypoglycemic user who lost consciousness and needed paramedic glucose. Serious injury to which the device may have contributed.

title: Meter read about 30 mmol/L; user took insulin; actual 6.1
rationale: A falsely high reading led to an insulin dose and hypoglycemia symptoms needing EMS. Malfunction likely to cause serious injury if it recurred; arguably serious injury already.

title: Meter would not power on; user blacked out; EMS glucose 536
rationale: Meter failure prevented testing; the user blacked out and was hospitalized with glucose 536 mg/dL. Malfunction with serious injury to which the device may have contributed.

title: Meter read 254 vs 191 and 198 on other meters; user injected 44 units
rationale: A large falsely high reading led to a 44-unit insulin dose. Malfunction likely to cause serious injury (hypoglycemia) if it recurred, even without treatment here.

title: Strips read 335 and 315 on non-diabetic spouse; insulin given; hypoglycemia
rationale: Falsely high readings (confirmed by a non-diabetic spouse reading 315) led to insulin and hypoglycemia. Malfunction likely to cause serious injury if it recurred.

title: IV vitamin C caused falsely high readings; insulin drip then hypoglycemia
rationale: Hypoglycemia needing IV dextrose after insulin given on falsely high readings. A known drug interference does not remove reportability when the device may have contributed.

title: Meter showed HI; actual glucose about 930; ICU
rationale: HI is the correct result for glucose of about 930 mg/dL, above the measuring range, so the device may have worked as intended. Serious injury occurred; whether the HI indication or labeling contributed to delay needs judgment.

title: Death after meter failures and incompatible strips; no link alleged
rationale: A death followed an inability to test, but with serious comorbidities, incompatible strips, refused care, and no link alleged. Whether the meter may have contributed requires judgment.

title: Meter changed its own date and time
rationale: No injury. A meter that resets its date and time can misattribute readings in the history used to adjust therapy; some manufacturers treat this as a reportable malfunction, others as low risk.

title: Back-to-back readings vary widely; no symptoms
rationale: Back-to-back variation of roughly 20-25% may exceed accuracy specs, but no symptoms, no treatment decision, and home technique unknown. Investigate before deciding.

title: Review: inaccurate in the cold; insulin overdoses alleged
rationale: An alleged link between inaccurate readings and insulin overdoses is a potential serious injury, but severity, treatment, and timing are unknown. Requires follow-up; lean reportable once details are confirmed.

title: Review: meter read up to 4.5 mmol/L above lab during glucose test
rationale: A 4.5 mmol/L discrepancy is well outside typical accuracy specs, but there is no harm, and timing and sample type (capillary vs venous) during the tolerance test are uncontrolled. Investigate.

title: All strips from one pack gave an error; another pack worked
rationale: Strips failed with an error and gave no result, so the failure was obvious and fail-safe. No incorrect reading, no harm. Complaint and lot investigation, not an MDR.

title: Pharmacy dispensed wrong control solution; look-alike bottles
rationale: Dispensing error with look-alike packaging, caught before harm; no device malfunction or injury. A human factors and complaint issue, not an MDR.

title: Review: about half of tests fail with an error code
rationale: Frequent error codes waste strips but give no result, so no incorrect reading reaches the user. No harm described. Complaint and trend, not an MDR.

title: Review: batteries last only two to three days
rationale: Battery life complaint; the meter still works when powered and gives no incorrect results. No harm. Complaint and trend.

title: Review: profile won't save; Bluetooth hard to pair
rationale: Connectivity and app usability issue with no effect on readings and no harm. Complaint, not an MDR.

title: Review: small buttons, needs a large blood drop
rationale: Usability complaint (size, buttons, sample volume) with no incorrect readings or harm. Complaint and possible human factors input, not an MDR.

title: Patient found unresponsive; oximeter not alarming
rationale: Death with an alleged failure to alarm. Information reasonably suggests the device may have caused or contributed; sensor placement is speculation and does not rule out device contribution.

title: Child died on monitoring; staff allege alarm failed
rationale: Death where staff allege the alarm did not work. A possible use error does not remove reportability when information suggests the device may have contributed.

title: Damaged control dial; patient died; no link alleged
rationale: A death occurred, but no information suggests device contribution. Whether a damaged control dial could affect alarms or settings is unknown at intake. Expert judgment needed.

title: Monitor kept showing SpO2 after patient died
rationale: The death is not attributed to the device. But displaying SpO2 values with no pulse is a malfunction that could delay recognition of arrest if it recurred, which argues reportable malfunction.

title: Newborn died; monitor showed normal values with no heartbeat
rationale: The monitor displayed false normal values for up to 20 minutes while there was no cardiac activity. That may have delayed intervention; a reported clinical cause of death does not rule out device contribution.

title: Monitor read 100% while patient was hypoxic; ICU transfer
rationale: Falsely normal reading in a hypoxic patient (ABG 68%) requiring ICU transfer. Serious injury to which the device may have contributed; detection by other means does not remove reportability.

title: Sensor blister progressed to fingertip blackening
rationale: Tissue injury requiring plastic surgery referral is a serious injury. A possible use factor (sensor left in place) does not remove reportability.

title: Home probe overheated and burned child's foot
rationale: Even if a first-degree burn is not a serious injury, probe overheating is a malfunction that would be likely to cause serious injury if it recurred, especially on a child.

title: Child coded at home; parents say no alarm
rationale: Life-threatening event with an alleged failure to alarm. The reporting clock starts at awareness; waiting for device return is not a basis to defer.

title: Tissue oximeter channels swapped; treatment changed
rationale: Mislabeled readings led to medication and fluid changes. Treatment based on erroneous device information is a malfunction likely to cause serious injury if it recurred.

title: CO-oximeter read 1% CO; actual carboxyhemoglobin 43%
rationale: Missing life-threatening carbon monoxide poisoning is a malfunction likely to cause death or serious injury if it recurred. Accurate SpO2 and timely transport do not offset it.

title: Handheld oximeter gave no readings before use
rationale: Total failure found before use, no patient. An obvious failure is often judged unlikely to cause serious injury, but if it recurred during monitoring it could. Root cause unknown at intake. (The manufacturer filed an MDR after investigation.)

title: Consumer oximeter reads about 10% low vs cleared device
rationale: A 10-point low bias is outside typical accuracy specs, but there is no harm, a single uncontrolled consumer comparison, and no confirmed malfunction. Needs investigation before a reportability call.

title: Online review: inaccurate readings, poor finger fit
rationale: Vague inaccuracy tied to poor finger contact, with no injury, no data, and no medical decision. Investigate and trend as a complaint; not an MDR on current information.

title: Consumer oximeter heats up with burning smell
rationale: Overheating on a finger-worn device is a potential burn and fire hazard, which argues reportable malfunction. But no injury, an unverified consumer report, and the cause may be the batteries. Needs investigation.

title: Sold as new but arrived scratched and used
rationale: Cosmetic and condition issue with no malfunction or injury. Handle as a complaint and a possible distribution issue, not an MDR.

title: Wrong brand shipped; not used
rationale: Order fulfillment issue; device not used; no malfunction or injury. A suspected counterfeit would be a separate investigation, not an MDR on these facts.

title: Lanyard strap missing from package
rationale: Missing accessory, device works, no injury. Complaint handling and trending, possibly CAPA if recurring, but not an MDR.

title: Consumer questions labeling and marketing claims
rationale: No adverse event or malfunction. A labeling and promotion compliance concern for regulatory review, not a medical device report.

title: Forwarded article on accuracy in darker skin
rationale: General literature concern with no specific device, patient, or event. Relevant to post-market surveillance and risk management, not an individual MDR.
